sec.title: Background & Aims
sec.p: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) exhibits diverse aetiologies and molecular heterogeneity, with a median 5-year overall survival of <70% due to high recurrence rates following curative-intent surgery. This study investigated the complex tumour microenvironment (TME) in HCC and explored interactions between various cell types and their roles in disease recurrence.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: Using a multi-omics approach on multi-region samples of surgically resected HCC from the PLANet 1.0 cohort (NCT03267641), we performed spatial transcriptomics on 17 tissue samples from four patients and bulk RNA sequencing on 329 sectors from 90 patients. Findings were validated using immunofluorescence and multiplex immunohistochemistry.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Our analysis revealed extensive intra- and intertumour gene expression heterogeneity and identified a specific subset of endothelial cells (ECs), INTS6+ ECs, enriched and spatially colocalised with tumour cells in primary tumours from patients with recurrence (p = 0.021, n = 49). A significant ANGPTL4–SDC1 ligand–receptor interaction was identified between INTS6+ ECs and tumour cells. Notably, INTS6+ ECs were enriched in microvascular invasion regions and spatially colocalised with tumour cells in patients with recurrence (p = 0.036, n = 53). These findings highlight endothelial–tumour cell interactions within the TME as potential therapeutic targets.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: INTS6+ ECs are enriched in microvascular invasion regions and spatially colocalised with tumour cells in recurrent HCC, suggesting a potential role in disease recurrence and representing a promising therapeutic target within the TME.

sec.title: Impact and implications
sec.p: The spatial co-localisation of cell types plays a significant role in the recurrence of hepatocellular carcinoma. In this study, we have pinpointed a particular group of endothelial cells, known as INTS6+ endothelial cells, which are spatially colocalised with tumour cells and enriched in microvascular invasion regions in patients experiencing recurrence. These discoveries highlight novel therapeutic targets that focus on endothelial cell interactions within the tumour microenvironment to prevent recurrence and enhance overall patient survival.

list-item.p: Spatial transcriptomics uncovers extensive intratumoral heterogeneity across HCC patient tumours.
INTS6+ ECs upregulate inflammatory and hypoxic programs.
INTS6+ ECs are enriched in regions of microvascular invasion and co-localise with tumour cells in patients with recurrence.
INTS6+ ECs interact with tumour cells via the ANGPTL4-SDC1 axis, driving enhanced tumour invasiveness.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: While hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is the sixth most diagnosed cancer globally, it is the third most common cause of cancer-related deaths1 mainly because only around 20% of HCC cases are diagnosed at an early stage when treatment can be potentially curative.2 HCC develops from multiple aetiologies, the main ones being chronic hepatitis B/C infection and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD).3 The genetic landscape of HCC has been well characterised, with mutations in the promoter region of TERT representing the most common genetic aberrations.[4], [5], [6], [7] Globally, surgical resection is the main curative treatment modality for HCC;8 however, it is associated with a high recurrence rate. Recurrence after surgical resection in HCC occurs in a bimodal pattern with an early and higher peak at 1 year, primarily from micro-metastases from the primary tumour, and a second peak between 4-5 years from de novo cancer arising from the underlying liver disease.9,10 Surgical resection, even in early-stage HCC within the Milan criteria, confers only a modest 5-year overall survival (OS) of <70% and a 5-year recurrence-free survival of 35%.[11], [12], [13] Adjuvant therapies after curative intent surgical resection in HCC have shown limited efficacy,14 especially as there are no validated predictive biomarkers for HCC. A sufficiently granular understanding of changes in the HCC tumour microenvironment (TME) within the primary tumour is urgently required to enable the prediction of early recurrence15 and to help identify appropriate candidates for adjuvant therapy clinical trials.

Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) has been employed in several HCC studies to elucidate the cell types and states present within the HCC TME and link these features to clinically significant trajectories, such as recurrence and treatment response.[16], [17], [18], [19], [20], [21], [22] Sun et al. performed scRNA-seq analysis comparing HCC tumours from 12 treatment-naïve and 6 early-recurrence patients and observed that recurrent tumours exhibited enrichment of CD8+ T cells with low cytotoxicity, which may result in poor anti-tumour immunity and disease recurrence.23 However, the TME is a complex ecosystem comprising multiple cell types that interact within diverse microenvironments, including altered vasculature, immune predation, and nutrient deprivation.24 Furthermore, the spatial organisation of these cells in distinct compartments may influence the functional cell-cell interactions that drive tumour biology. For example, the presence of tertiary lymphoid structures, which are localised aggregates of immune cells within the tumour, has been associated with responses to immune checkpoint blockade in several cancer types.25 Therefore, a cellular and molecular map of the spatial resolution of the HCC TME correlated with clinical trajectories and response to therapy, including tumour recurrence after surgical resection, will complement the current understanding of disease biology and provide therapeutic avenues.

Several studies have explored the spatial architecture of the HCC TME, using rapidly evolving technologies such as 10x Visium, Stereo-seq, and NanoString CosMx and the field continues to evolve.[26], [27], [28], [29], [30] These studies demonstrated high levels of transcriptomic and copy number variations across the tumour boundary, which consists of non-tumour, leading-edge, and tumour regions. However, these studies do not employ multi-region sampling of the tumour core to investigate intratumoural heterogeneity. Single sampling of solid cancers has been shown to underappreciate tumour heterogeneity, and analyses of spatially distinct sites have unravelled significant genomic and molecular intratumoural heterogeneity.5,31,32 Such heterogeneity has important implications for inferring the clinical trajectories of tumours and their response to treatment and prognosis.33

The Precision Medicine in Liver Cancer across an Asia-Pacific Network study (PLANet 1.0, NCT03267641) was conceptualised to address the urgent unmet need for predictive biomarkers in HCC. This ongoing multinational, multidisciplinary, longitudinal study employs a strategy of multi-region sampling of surgically resected HCC and subsequent sampling of recurrent tumours to perform comprehensive molecular analysis. In this prospective HCC resection cohort study, patients were closely followed up after surgery until recurrence or death. The well-annotated clinical data (Table S1), together with the associated multi-omics data from the cohort, describe the heterogeneous intratumoural landscape and the natural trajectory of the disease.5,34,35 Our previous report from PLANet 1.0 cohort has shown that the re-emergence and co-localisation of fetal-associated PLVAP+/VEGFR2+ endothelial cells (ECs) and embryonic-like FOLR2+/CD163+ tumour-associated macrophages conferred an immunosuppressive environment in HCC, which was maintained by VEGF/NOTCH signalling.22 This observation provides insights into the co-localisation of specific biomarkers, cells, and metabolite densities, which may underpin aspects of tumour evolution and response to therapy.22

In this study, we leveraged surgically obtained samples from the PLANet 1.0 study to perform an unbiased spatial transcriptomic analysis. This study is the first to perform spatial transcriptomic analysis on multiple distinct regions of a tumour core, which allowed us to explore tumour ecosystem heterogeneity and annotate cell types, interaction networks, ligand-receptor interactions, and explore candidate biomarkers correlated with clinically meaningful outcomes. These findings provide a useful spatial, cellular, and molecular atlas to better understand the natural course of HCC after surgical resection with curative intent. We report novel enrichment and spatial proximity of integrator complex subunit 6 (INTS6+) ECs and tumour cells in primary tumours of patients with HCC who subsequently experienced tumour recurrence. A gene signature from INTS6+ ECs was significantly associated with time to recurrence (TTR) and OS in the PLANet 1.0 and The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) cohorts. Altogether, our study describes a spatial atlas associated with HCC recurrence after surgical resection and identifies a novel endothelial–tumour epithelium cellular co-localisation that has immense biological implications.

sec.title: Patient samples for 10x Genomics Visium spatial transcriptomics
sec.p: Multi-regional samples were obtained from resected HCC following a protocol as previously described.5,32 These samples were obtained from a subset of patients enrolled in the PLANet study (NCT03267641) conducted under the auspices of the AHCC (Asia-Pacific Hepatocellular Carcinoma) trials group. The PLANet recruitment criteria required patients to have no extrahepatic metastasis with R0 or R1 resection and a Child-Pugh score of ≤7 points without clinical ascites. The complete patient recruitment criteria are described in our previous report.5 This study was approved by the Central Institution Review Board of SingHealth (2016/2626 and 2018/2112), and written consent was obtained from all patients.

sec.title: Tumour sampling methodology
sec.p: The resected specimens were acquired immediately after surgical removal from the patient and transported on ice in a temperature-controlled cooler container to a pathologist, where each specimen was subjected to multi-region sampling through a grid sampling protocol.5 Non-tumour normal tissues were defined as segments at least 2 cm away from the tumour. The tumour was then cut through the capsule, photographed, and inspected for fibrosis, necrosis, haemorrhage, and cystic changes. Multiple sectors (regions) along one axis of a single tumour slice were harvested. After surgery and pathological evaluation, the samples were delivered in MACS buffer on ice. Upon arrival at the laboratory, the samples were removed from the buffer, cut into approximately 4-5 mm3 pieces, and embedded in optimal cutting temperature (OCT) compound.

sec.title: Collection and preparation of primary tumour samples
sec.p: Surgically resected samples were placed in MACS buffer and transported to the research laboratory. On arrival, samples were immediately embedded in OCT compound in a mold and frozen on dry ice before storing at -80 °C. Prior to performing tissue optimisation, 10 consecutive sections from each sample were obtained, RNA was extracted, and RNA Integrity Number analysis was performed using the Bioanalyzer RNA Nano or Pico Chip. Only samples with RIN ≥7.0 were used for spatial transcriptomic analysis on the 10X Genomics Visium platform.

sec.title: Determining optimal tissue permeabilisation conditions to ensure maximal mRNA recovery
sec.p: The permeabilisation time for each tissue was determined to ensure maximum recovery of mRNA. Tissue sections were placed on a Tissue Optimisation slide, fixed, and stained with H&E reagents prior to imaging. Before permeabilisation, the tissues were treated with 75 μl of Liberase™ for 15 min at 37 °C. The enzyme mix was removed, and the tissues were washed with 100 μl of 0.1X sodium saline citrate (SSC) buffer before tissue permeabilisation. Next, 70 μl of permeabilisation enzyme was added to each tissue for 5, 10, and 15 min. Permeabilisation results in the release of mRNA onto a poly(T) oligonucleotide in the capture areas. cDNA was then synthesised, and the fluorescent signal was determined. High-quality RNA from HEK293T cells was used as a positive control. The efficiency of permeabilisation was determined as the time required to achieve the strongest fluorescence intensity with minimal background. After cDNA synthesis, the tissue slide was immersed in 0.2x SSC buffer with 0.1% SDS, followed by 0.2x SSC buffer, and finally 0.1x SSC buffer. Fluorescence was imaged on the Cy3 channel at 10X magnification, and the time point with the most even and brightest fluorescence was determined to be the optimal permeabilisation condition. Based on this time point, multi-sector sectioning was performed at a thickness of 10-14 μm on a Visium slide and processed further.

sec.title: Tissue fixation, H&E staining, and imaging
sec.p: Once sectioned onto the Visium slide, the tissue sections were fixed in methanol for 30 min at -20 °C. The slides were then immersed in isopropanol for 1 min, followed by hematoxylin for 7 min, bluing buffer for 2 min, and eosin mix for 1 min at room temperature. After each staining step, the slides were washed with ultrapure water and incubated at 37 °C on a heat block for 1 min to dry. Coverslips were mounted using 85% glycerol and imaged using a Zeiss microscope at 20X magnification, as recommended by 10X Genomics.

sec.title: Tissue permeabilisation, reverse transcription, second-strand synthesis, denaturation, and cDNA amplification
sec.p: The stained slide was then placed in the Slide Cassette, and the permeabilisation enzyme was added at the optimised time point. The released poly(A) mRNA was captured using poly(dT) primers on the spots and washed with SSC buffer. Reverse transcription was then performed using the master mix containing the reagents on the Thermocycler Adaptor to generate spatially barcoded full-length cDNA from the recovered polyA mRNA. The cDNA was removed from the slide by incubating in 0.08 M potassium hydroxide for 5 min, and samples from each well were transferred to a strip tube with Tris-HCl (1M, pH 7.0). Next, 1 μl of the denatured sample was used for qPCR amplification to determine the sample Cq value. Next, cDNA synthesis was performed with the denatured sample using the cDNA Amplification Mix provided, and this mix was placed in a Thermocycler Adaptor for one cycle. The resulting cDNA was cleaned according to the instructions provided by 10X Genomics, involving incubation with SPRIselect beads and ethanol washes, before eluting in EB buffer. The quantity and quality of the cDNA were determined using an Agilent Bioanalyzer High-Sensitivity Chip, and the cDNA was diluted tenfold prior to loading onto the chip.

sec.title: Illumina sequencing library generation
sec.p: The sequencing library was prepared according to the protocol provided by 10X Genomics. Briefly, 10 μl of cDNA from the previous step was used for enzymatic fragmentation, end-repair, A-tailing, and size selection using SPRIselect beads. Sequencing adaptors were ligated, double-sided size selection and clean-up were performed, and sample index (Dual Index Kit TT Set A) PCR was conducted before a final double-sided size selection and clean-up. Library quality and quantity were assessed using the Agilent High Sensitivity DNA Chip, and the final quantitation was performed using Qubit. Sequencing libraries were then submitted to a local sequencing partner and sequenced at a depth of 25,000 read pairs per spot, multiplied by the estimated fudicial frame coverage of the tissue on the Illumina HiSeq platform.

sec.title: Raw data preprocessing
sec.p: Visium spatial RNA sequenced reads were analysed using the space ranger pipeline (version: 1.3.0, 10X genomics) to align the reads to the hg38 reference genome and generate gene-spot matrices corresponding to H&E images from each tissue. Visium combines spatial algorithms with the widely used RNA-seq aligner, STAR. Initial inspection of the data was performed using the Loupe browser (6.3.0, 10X Genomics).

sec.title: Quality control
sec.p: The filtered featured matrix (UMI counts), spatial coordinates CSV file, scale-factor JSON file, and H&E image were imported into the Python package squidpy using the sc.read_visium function. Quality control was performed to remove low quality spots that consisted of less than 200 genes or mitochondrial percentages >5%. Genes that were expressed in fewer than three spots were removed. Mitochondrial and ribosomal genes were excluded from the analysis.

sec.title: Normalisation, dimension reduction, clustering, and ligand-receptor analysis
sec.p: Gene expression count data were normalised initially using sc.pp.normalize_total, and subsequently followed by log1p normalisation using the squidpy package.36 The top 2,000 highly variable genes were selected based on the expression mean and variance. Normalised gene expression data were subjected to principal component analysis (PCA) using the first 30 PCA components, shared nearest neighbourhood graphing, and Leiden clustering. The Leiden algorithm is an improved version of the Louvain algorithm and outperforms other clustering algorithms for single-cell datasets.37,38 Therefore, we used Leiden clustering to cluster the spots based on gene expression. Dimensionality reduction was performed using uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP), and Squidpy was implemented for clustering and dimension reduction analysis.

sec.title: Microvascular invasion (MVI) annotation
sec.p: The HCC resection specimens were examined in details by clinical pathologists and reported using the College of American Pathologists protocol for the “Examination of Specimens from patients with Hepatocellular Carcinoma” version 4.1.0.0. For smaller tumours up to 2 cm in size, the entire tumour was subjected to histological evaluation. For larger tumours, at least one section per cm of tumour was evaluated. With respect to venous and vascular invasion, gross examination for macroscopic venous invasion was performed with relevant sections submitted for histological confirmation, if present. Sections of tumour with adjacent non-tumour tissue were also examined for microscopic vascular invasion. The pathologist followed these criteria to annotate the MVI regions.

For the Visium spatial transcriptomics data, the corresponding H&E images were scanned using an Olympus microscope and analysed with QuPath (v0.6.0). Digital images were reviewed by clinical pathologists who were blinded to the spatial transcriptomic results. Several histological features were annotated using various colour schemes of the QuPath annotation function for tumour, fibrosis and immune cell regions as well as MVI regions. Histological findings, such as MVI, were superimposed with INTS6+ ECs and tumour cells, indicating that MVI regions were enriched with INTS6+ ECs and tumour cells.

sec.title: Multiplex immunofluorescence (mIF) assay
sec.p: Tissues were sectioned on Polysine slides (Shandon Thermo Scientific 25 x 77 mm x 1.0 mm Ref #6776215) with 10 μM thickness and then were deparaffinised and rehydrated by immersing the slides in the following solutions in separate chambers for 2 min for each step: 100% Xylene, 100% Xylene, 50% Xylene+50% Ethanol, 100% Ethanol, 90% ethanol, 80% ethanol, 70% ethanol, and distilled water. Slides were transferred into the pre-heated Tris-EDTA buffer at 95 °C for 45 min, and tissue section slides were immersed in distilled water to wash and cool down. Slides were blotted dry by flicking the slides gently, and blocking buffer (2% BSA in PBST) was added to cover the entire tissue section, followed by incubation for 1 h at room temperature. After blocking, the blocking buffer was removed, and samples were incubated with primary antibodies (INTS6 1:50; CD31 1:50, STMN1 1:100) at 4 °C for overnight. The next day, primary antibodies were removed, and the slides were washed with PBST for 5 min three times. Then, the secondary antibody mixture was added to the sections, followed by 1-hour incubation in a humidified chamber at room temperature in the dark. Slides were washed with PBST for 5 min three times and then stained with DAPI for 10 min. The slides were rinsed with PBST and mounted with a mounting medium and coverslip. Stained slides were dried overnight to remove the excess mounting medium and were imaged using Zeiss LSM800 Upright microscope. For each slide, at least 5 regions of interest (ROIs) were chosen based on their vascular morphology, CD31 and INTS6 expression as a primary observation, followed by STMN1 expression as the next parameter.

sec.title: Multiplex immunohistochemistry (mIHC) assay
sec.p: mIHC staining was performed on 4 μm thick formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) human HCC tissue sections using Leica Bond Max auto stainer (Leica Biosystems, Melbourne, Australia), Bond Refine Detection Kit (Leica Biosystems, Newcastle Upon Tyne, UK) and PANO 7-plex TSA IHC Kit (Panovue, Beijing, China). In brief, FFPE tissue sections were subjected to repeated cycles of heat-induced epitope retrieval, incubation with primary antibodies (CD31 (#M0823 Dako), CD34 (#M7165 Dako), INTS6 (Merck HPA001552), HepPar1 (Cell Signalling #96422), GPC3 (Abcam #ab207080)), secondary antibodies (Bond Refine Kit) and tyramide signal amplification (TSA) (Panovue, Beijing, China). DAPI (Panovue, Beijing, China) is applied as a nuclear counterstain. Images were captured using an automated imaging system, Axioscan 7 (Zeiss, Germany). Multiplex immunohistochemistry was performed on tissue from a total of 50 patients, including 25 with recurrent and 25 with non-recurrent disease (Table S3), using the COMET system (Lunaphore).

sec.title: Image analysis and quantification
sec.p: QuPath (v0.6.0) was used for the visualisation and cell segmentation of mIF images. To identify INTS6+CD31+ cells that colocalise to the STMN1 region, we performed watershed-based segmentation with the default parameters and exported the resultant cell detection measurements for downstream analysis. To ensure accurate cell identification, nuclei with DAPI intensity greater than two times the median absolute deviation (MAD) from the median were retained. The same approach was used to classify cells as positive for each of the three imaging markers (INTS6, CD31 and STMN1) across all imaged ROIs. For each patient, we report the median proportion of cells co-expressing all three markers (INTS6, CD31 and STMN1) across all imaged ROIs to obtain a patient-level estimate.

To quantify the spatial colocalization of INTS6+ ECs and tumour cells, watershed-based segmentation was first performed on each whole-slide image using default parameters with a detection threshold of 1,500. Three independent random forest classifiers were trained to detect INTS6+, CD31+, and HepPar1+ cells. After manual verification of classifier performance for each image, the classifiers were sequentially applied to all segmented cells across the whole-slide images. Spatial relationships between the INTS6+CD31+ endothelial cells and HepPar1+ tumour cells were computed using the detectionCentroidDistances() function in QuPath, which calculates the pairwise centroid distances between neighbouring cells. The resulting measurements were subsequently exported for downstream analysis. An INTS6+ endothelial cell was defined as adjacent to a HepPar1+ tumour cell if the centroid-to-centroid distance was less than 5 μm. For each sample, the proportion of adjacent INTS6+ ECs was calculated as the number of INTS6+ ECs within 5 μm of a HepPar11+ tumour cell divided by the total number of detected cells. Statistical comparisons between the recurrent and non-recurrent patients were conducted with the two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum test, with a significance threshold of p value <0.05.

sec.title: Migration assay
sec.p: Human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs, cat #C0035C), human large vessel endothelial basal medium (cat# M200500), and low serum growth supplement (cat# S00310) were purchased from Life Technologies. HUVECs were seeded at a density of 100,000 cells per well in a 24-well plate and incubated for 48 h before transfection with small-interfering RNA (siRNA) against INTS6 for 48 h siRNA duplex sequences used for experiment are mentioned as follow: INTS6 siRNA1: 5’- rArGrA rArArA rCrCrA rUrGrC rArArC rGrUrU rUrArU rGrAA T –3', 5’- rArUrU rCrArU rArArA rCrGrU rUrGrC rArUrG rGrUrU rUrUrC rUrUrU –3'; siRNA2: 5’- rGrGrU rArUrA rUrGrC rUrGrG rUrCrA rCrUrU rUrCrG rArAG A –3', 5’- rUrCrU rUrCrG rArArA rGrUrG rArCrC rArGrC rArUrA rUrArC rCrUrG-3'; siRNA3: 5’- rGrCrG rGrUrA rGrArG rArCrC rUrUrC rArUrG rArArG rCrUC C –3', 5’- rGrGrA rGrCrU rUrCrA rUrGrA rArGrG rUrCrU rCrUrA rCrCrG rCrGrC –3'. As siRNA1 provided the greatest suppression of INTS6 expression, this duplex was selected for the migration assay. SNU387, SNU449, HLF, and HUH7 cells were seeded in transwell plates with HUVECs transfected with scrambled control and INTS6 siRNA. Cells were incubated for 24 h before fixation in paraformaldehyde and crystal violet and imaged using a Zeiss Axios Observer 7 microscope. For the ANGPTL4 migration assay, the ANGPTL4 CDS was first cloned into the pLJM1-EGFP lentiviral plasmid backbone to overexpress the ANGPTL4 gene. The control plasmid or the plasmid overexpressing ANGPTL4 was then transfected into HEK293T cells using Lipofectamine LTX. The media was changed 8 h after transfection, and the enriched media were collected 24 and 48 h later. The SNU387, SNU449, SNU475, and HLF cells were then seeded in transwell over the 24-well plate containing control media or ANGPTL4-enriched media. Cells were incubated for 24 h before being fixed in paraformaldehyde and crystal violet and imaged using the Zeiss Axios Observer 7 microscope.

sec.title: INTS6 knockdown and control in the HUVEC cell line
sec.p: 300,000 HUVECs were seeded in a 6-well plate tissue culture dish, and lentiviral soap of Control shRNA or INTS6 shRNAs was added to the cells the next day after plating. The media was changed 8 h after infection, and the cells were incubated in a humidified incubator at 37 °C for 3 additional days. After incubation, cells were trypsinised, and the cell pellets were subjected to total RNA isolation using TRIzol, followed by DNase treatment. The RNA concentration was measured by nanodrop and bioanalyzer, and a total of 500 ng RNA was subjected to directional mRNA library preparation prior to the mRNA sequencing procedure using the NovaSeq PE150 platform.

sec.title: Bulk RNA-seq analysis for INTS6 knockdown and control raw data processing and quality control
sec.p: Fastq files were processed with the nf-core RNA-seq pipeline version 3.19.0. Sequenced reads were aligned to hg38 reference genome using STAR. The raw count and transcripts per million (TPM) of each gene were quantified by RSEM. DESeq2 was used to perform differential expression analysis of the sequenced data. Only genes with at least one read found in 20% of the total samples were retained for the analysis. Differentially expressed genes were defined using the cut-off values of |log2 fold change| >2 and adjusted p value <0.05. Web based tool Enrichr was used for pathway enrichment analysis with the MsigDB Hallmark 2020 database.39,40

sec.title: Spatial co-localisation analysis
sec.p: We employed the CellTrek package41 and utilised scRNA-seq data from a recent study by Liu et al.29 to deconvolute the Visium spatial spots. The SColoc module was used to to capture spatial co-localisation of different cell types. This module summarises the CellTrek results into graph abstraction. Spatial dissimilarity between cell types was calculated using the Kullback-Leibler divergence method with default parameters. The SCmodule constructs a minimum spanning tree to represent the spatial co-localisation of cell types.

sec.title: Ligand–receptor analysis
sec.p: CellChat42 was utilised to interrogate the ligand-receptor interactions among various cell types using single-cell data. We selected the CellChatDB database, specifically focusing on human species, to access curated ligand–receptor interactions collected from the literature. By default, CellChat employs a statistically robust mean method known as the trimean to compute the average gene expression for each cell group, resulting in fewer interactions compared to other methods. We excluded cell groups with fewer than ten cells from the cell-cell communication analysis. The results were displayed in a chord plot.

sec.title: Survival analysis
sec.p: To determine whether spatial gene expression is associated with clinical characteristics and trajectory, and specifically with recurrent-free survival, we generated bulk gene expression profiles and applied them to bulk RNA-seq data from 90 patients in the PLANet cohort (including the four patients in this study) (Table S1) for analysis using the R package Survminer. At the time of analysis, these patients either developed HCC recurrence, died, or were followed up for at least 3 years without recurrence, with recurrence-free survival assessed as described previously.5 The mean expression of the INTS6+ EC gene signature was generated, which is significantly associated with OS.

sec.title: Overall cohort composition
sec.p: Despite utilising multiple samples for 10X Visium, issues with RNA recovery during permeabilisation restricted our final dataset to seventeen well-processed specimens from four patients. These samples were meticulously selected to represent a diverse range of patient populations and recurrence statuses. Although further spatial transcriptomics analysis is currently unfeasible, we expanded our validation studies specifically through mIHC and mIF, to improve statistical rigour. We employed 49 HCC patient FFPE slides (24 recurrent and 25 non-recurrent) for mIHC to analyse the colocalization of INTS6+ ECs with the tumour cells. Additionally, 53 HCC patient FFPE slides (27 recurrent and 26 non-recurrent) were examined using mIF to analyse the colocalization of INTS6+ ECs in the MVI regions.

sec.title: Experimental design, clinico-pathological characteristics, and clinical trajectory of the study
sec.p:
Utilising the PLANet1.0 patient samples, we conducted bulk RNA-seq for 329 samples from 90 patients, where a subset of samples were used for spatial transcriptomics analysis to determine the unique spatial, molecular, and cellular ecosystem of HCC with recurrence (n = 3) and without recurrence (n = 1), followed by validation assays using immunoflourescence (n = 53 patients) and immunohistochemistry (n = 49 patients) (Fig. 1A). We conducted a spatial transcriptomic analysis of multiple sectors per primary tumour (Fig. 1B) from patients with HCC treated with curative intent surgical resection who were without recurrence at 60 months after surgery (A009) and patients who had early tumour recurrences between 3.6 to 14.0 months (C008, B013, C004). All patients had well-annotated clinical data (Fig. 1C). These patients from the PLANet 1.0 longitudinal cohort study5 comprised both chronic viral hepatitis B-positive and -negative individuals. Where possible, we profiled adjacent non-tumour tissue (‘normal’) as a reference. Each primary tumour was sampled from 2-5 distinct regions, and at least one section per region was obtained for spatial transcriptomic analysis (Fig. 1B). In patient C004, we examined both the primary and recurrent tumour sectors.Fig. 1
Study design and patient cohort.
(A) Schematic overview of the cohort and HCC patient-derived sample utilisation. Bulk RNA sequencing was performed on a cohort of 329 samples from 90 patient samples. The samples were then used for subsequent analyses, including spatial transcriptomics (n = 4) to identify unique spatial cellular ecosystem of recurrent HCC, as well as immunofluorescence (n = 53) and immunohistochemistry (n = 49) for validation assays. (B) Workflow schema of spatial transcriptomic analysis performed on HCC tumours from PLANet 1.0 cohort. After surgical resection, sectors marked and gridded as part of pathology evaluation. Tissues were then snapped frozen and embedded in OCT compound. Fourteen-micron sections were cut onto a tissue optimization slide to determine the permeabilization time to maximize RNA yield. Tissue sections were then placed on the gene expression slide and RNA recovered, before generating libraries for sequencing and downstream bioinformatic analysis. (C) Computed tomography scans of primary tumours, schema of primary and recurrent tumour location, gross tumour images, and clinical information for patients A009, B013, C008 and C004 are provided. HCC, hepatocellular carcinoma; OCT, optimal cutting temperature.Fig. 1

All four patients were Child-Pugh A, underwent R0 resection (resection margins were free from macroscopic and microscopic tumours), and were closely followed up after surgical resection. Of these patients, C008, B013, and C004 had recurrences at 3.6, 6.3, and 14 months after surgery, respectively (Fig. 1C). All three patients with tumour recurrence had unfavourable clinicopathological features that predisposed them to early recurrence, namely tumour size >5 cm (11.3 cm, 6.7 cm, and 6.9 cm, respectively), presence of satellite nodules (C008, B013), higher TNM stage (IIIA, IIIA, and IB), respectively), or alpha-fetoprotein >400 ng/ml (C004). All three tumours were Edmonson Grade 2 and positive for chronic hepatitis B viral infection. Interestingly, patient A009, who was hepatitis B/C virus-negative and recurrence-free 60 months post-surgery, also presented with unfavourable clinicopathological features: a 7.6 cm Edmonson grade 3 tumour with microvascular invasion and an alpha-fetoprotein level of 2,203 ng/ml at the time of resection (Fig. 1C).

sec.title: Spatial transcriptomics reveals extensive intratumoral molecular heterogeneity across HCC patient tumours
sec.p: To gain insights into the intratumoural molecular heterogeneity (ITH) in HCC tumours, we first performed gene expression-based clustering of the Visium spots. We observed a remarkable degree of ITH across the tumour sectors in all four patients (Fig. S1A–D), ranging from 7 to 13 annotated gene expression clusters per patient sample. Based on the top five differentially expressed genes (DEGs) for each cluster, we observed that several clusters expressed signatures characteristic of specific cell types in the HCC tumour microenvironment (Fig. S2). For instance, cluster 0 of C008 sector 1 included genes such as ALB, TTR, and APOA1, which represent hepatocytes; cluster 4 (CD74, C1QA, C1QB) represented macrophages; and cluster 6 (ACTA2, TAGLN, MCAM) represented smooth muscle or endothelial cells (Fig. S2C). Cluster 2 from this patient (SAA1, SAA2, CRP), which represents a subset of damaged hepatocytes, was also identified in patient B013 sector 2 (B013 T2) as cluster 4, both of whom experienced recurrence. Interestingly, this cluster was not present in patient A009, who had no recurrence (Fig. S2). Consistent with this observation, elevated SAA1 and SAA2 expression levels were also observed in intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma with poor prognosis in a separate study.28 To validate the accuracy of our cluster-based annotations, we performed histopathological evaluation of our H&E images from all the tumour sectors analysed. We found very high concordance between our molecular annotation (Fig. S1A–D), and the histological annotations provided by the pathologist. For instance, in patient B013 sector 1 (B013T1), the regions associated with immune cells, fibrosis, and blood vessels/haemorrhage showed good concordance between our annotation and pathologist’s annotation (Fig. S1E). Similarly, in patient C008 sector 2 (C008T2), the fibrotic regions associated with fibroblasts were concordant between our annotation and that of the pathologist (Fig. S1E).

To further characterise the heterogeneity in cell abundances of tumour, stromal and immune populations across tumour sectors, we employed an orthogonal approach using the AUCell package43 to annotate the cell types present in our datasets, leveraging the cell type expression signatures from a publicly available scRNA-seq dataset by Liu et al.29 AUCell enrichment scoring revealed marked heterogeneity in the abundance of cell types across tumour sectors of the same patient and across tumours of different patients (Fig. 2A). For instance, hepatocytes comprised 35% of the tissue in sector 1 and only 7% in sector 3 of the same tumour in the C008 patient. Variability in other cell types, such as myeloid cells (17–33%), fibroblasts (5–12%), ECs (10.9–26.3%), and CD8 T cells (9–17%), was also apparent across all patient sectors. Certain cell types, such as regulatory CD4 T cells (0.9–3.5%) and exhausted CD8 T cells (0–2.7%), comprised a smaller proportion of the entire tumour across patients. Therefore, multi-region sampling is essential for capturing ITH and providing a comprehensive understanding of tumour complexity. This approach is supported by the recently described ‘bad apple’ concept, where the most aggressive tumour region (i.e. B013T4, C008T2, and C004P) dictates the clinical trajectory.44 Taken together, these findings suggest that the precise tumour sector collected for a study can alter the readout of cellular ecosystems, with implications for the design, execution, and interpretation of single-cell studies.Fig. 2
Cellular ecosystem of multi-sector HCC.
(A) AUcell enrichment for each spot of the Visium slide using single cell annotation data from Liu et al. The percentages of each cell type in each sector are depicted as a cumulative bar plot. (B) Distribution of CXCL10 macrophage subsets across tumour sectors. (C,D) Distribution of fibroblast subsets across tumour sectors. (E-G) Distribution of endothelial cell subsets across tumour sectors. HCC, hepatocellular carcinoma; N, adjacent normal; R, recurrent tumour; T, primary tumour sector.Fig. 2

sec.title: A distinct INTS6+ endothelial cell subset is associated with tumour recurrence
sec.p: Since we observed sizeable variations in myeloid, fibroblast, and EC populations, we further analysed the subpopulations of these cell types using the annotation provided by Liu et al. This analysis revealed that the CXCL10+ macrophage population was enriched in tumour sectors from patient A009 (Fig. 2B), whereas cancer-associated fibroblasts and myofibroblasts were enriched in patients B013, C008, and C004, who experienced early disease recurrence (Fig. 2C,D). CXCL10+ macrophages are crucial for inducing antitumour inflammation and enhancing the response to immune checkpoint blockade.[45], [46], [47] It is also worth noting that the primary tumour from patient C004 had a higher abundance of both cancer-associated fibroblasts and myofibroblasts than the recurrent tumour. We further grouped the ECs into three distinct populations. Interestingly, we observed a trend for lower INTS6+ and PLVAP+ ECs in patient A009, relative to patients B013, C008, and C004 (Fig. 2E,F). PLVAP+ ECs have been proposed as therapeutic targets and were recently identified as components of the oncofetal niche that creates an immunosuppressive environment in HCC.22,48 However, the role of INTS6+ ECs in the recurrence of HCC or any other carcinomas remain unexplored. Given their association with recurrence in our spatial transcriptomics cohort, this prompted us to further analyse the function of INTS6+ ECs. Altogether, these findings suggest that differences in the stromal population of tumours across geographically distinct sectors are associated with disease recurrence.

sec.title: Tumour-stroma neighbourhood analysis reveals INTS6+/PLVAP+ ECs in close proximity to tumour cells in the primary tumour of patients with recurrence
sec.p:
To understand how cellular organisation differs spatially between primary tumours in patients with and without disease recurrence, we assessed the spatial co-localisation of cell types associated with recurrence. We observed that at least one sector from multi-region samples of primary tumours from the three patients who had disease recurrence showed close proximity of INTS6+ and PLVAP+ ECs to tumour cells, and this was not observed in any of the tumour sectors from the recurrence-free patient A009 (Fig. 3A). Our analysis also revealed close proximity between INTS6+ ECs and subsets of dendritic cells (DC1/DC2) in the primary tumours of three patients with recurrence (Fig. 3B,D) which was not seen in patient without recurrence (Fig. 3E).Fig. 3
Cellular neighbourhood analysis identifies INTS6+ ECs in close proximity to tumour cells in patients with recurrence.
(A) Summarised heatmap showing INTS6+ ECs and tumour cells in close proximity. The legend scale ranges from 0 to 1. The grey colour indicates the value 0, which suggests there is no interaction between them whereas the orange to red colour shows that there is interaction among these cell types. (B-E) Aggressive tumour sectors and one sector from A009 to demonstrate the cellular network as predicted by CellTrek analysis. (F) The Spatial feature plot for INTS6+ ECs, represented by black spots and tumour cells, indicated by red spots, is depicted on the superimposed H&E-stained image for samples B013T4, C008T2, and C004P. (G) Heatmap summarising upregulated signalling pathways in aggressive tumour sectors relative to the sectors from a non-recurrent patient (A009). (H) H&E whole-slide image from patient HEP0853. (I) Multiplexed immunohistochemisty staining for HepPar1, INTS6 and CD31 (performed on a section adjacent to the H&E slide). (J) Top: Panel of single-channel images, followed by the corresponding composite image for the boxed region of interest. Bottom: DAPI nuclei and cell segmentation, followed by binary classification outputs for each channel. For the composite image, classifiers were applied sequentially, and a single segmented object could be positive for multiple markers. Red indicates negative labels, while other colors denote positive labels. (K) Left: An INTS6+ EC (olive triangle marking the cell centroid) positioned adjacent to an INTS6+ CD31- cell (yellow square), with no HepPar1+ tumour cell present within a 5 μm radius. Right: An INTS6+ EC located within a 5 μm radius from a HepPar11+ tumour cell (magenta square marking the cell centroid). (L) Quantification of the proportion of INTS6+ ECs that are adjacent to HepPar1+ tumour cells in the patients with non-recurrent (n = 25) vs. recurrent (n = 24) HCC. For this analysis, the entire WSI for each sample was processed. HepPar1+ tumour cells within 5 μm of an INTS6+ ECs were defined as adjacent. CAF, cancer-associated fibroblast; EC, endothelial cell; HCC, hepatocellular carcinoma; MAIT, mucosal-associated invariant T. Statistical comparisons between the recurrent and non-recurrent patients were conducted with the two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum test, with a significance threshold of p value <0.05.Fig. 3

We then investigated the tumour sectors containing close proximity of INTS6+ ECs with tumour cells, which could potentially contribute to the aggressiveness of the tumour sectors (B013T4, C008T2, C004P). By analysing bulk RNA-seq data obtained from these sectors, DEGs were identified by comparing each individual aggressive sector with patient A009’s five sectors. Ingenuity Pathway Analysis was performed for three sets of DEGs, and the common upregulated pathways were selected based on p values <0.05 and enrichment scores >1.5. The upregulated pathways identified in this analysis highlight the complex interplay of signalling mechanisms contributing to tumour recurrence. These pathways encompass various aspects of tumour biology, including cell proliferation, survival, migration, invasion, angiogenesis, immune evasion, and the tumour microenvironment (Fig. 3G). Taken together, these data suggest that aggressive tumour sectors where INTS6+ ECs are in close proximity to tumour cells exhibited a distinct yet complex set of signalling pathway networks that may be involved in cancer recurrence and may be associated with poor disease outcomes.

Next, as an orthogonal method to validate the spatial co-localisation of INTS6+ ECs with tumour cells in HCC recurrence, we performed mIHC on FFPE primary tumour samples from an independent set of 50 patients (25 with recurrence and 25 without recurrence) in our PLANet 1.0 cohort (Fig. 3H-J). We observed that INTS6+CD31+ ECs were preferentially located in close proximity (within 5 μm) to HepPar1+ tumour cells in patients with recurrence compared to those without recurrence (Fig. 3K,L). These findings highlight the potential importance of the spatial interactions of INTS6+ ECs with tumour cells in the context of disease recurrence. Overall, the observed association between INTS6+ ECs and tumour cell co-localisation and disease recurrence suggests a possible role of INTS6+ ECs in the pathology of HCC recurrence, warranting further investigation.

sec.title: INTS6+ ECs are a unique EC subpopulation, with a gene signature associated with HCC recurrence
sec.p:
Our spatial transcriptomic and mIHC analysis revealed a novel association between the proximity of INTS6+ ECs and tumour hepatocytes enriched in primary tumours of patients with recurrence. First, to ensure that INTS6+ ECs retained their endothelial identity, we quantified the expression of classical endothelial markers in these cells compared to all other cell types. We found that the endothelial cell marker genes, such as CD31 (PECAM1) and CD34, were significantly upregulated in INTS6+ ECs relative to other cell types within the B013T4, C008T2, and C004P samples (Fig. S4). This is also visually evident from the expression of CD31 in the INTS6+ ECs relative to ALB+ tumour cells (Fig. 3F). This finding substantiates the identity of INTS6+ ECs as bona fide ECs. To determine whether INTS6+ ECs represent a distinct endothelial subpopulation, we performed trajectory analysis using Monocle49 on the single-cell dataset. We observed that the INTS6+ ECs formed a separate group from PLVAP+, TFF3+, or proliferating ECs (Fig. 4B), indicating that they constitute a unique endothelial subpopulation.Fig. 4
Patients with high expression of INTS6+ EC gene signature exhibit poor prognosis for overall survival and recurrence in HCC cohort.
(A) Top 10 most differentially expressed genes between INTS6+ ECs and other cell types from the Liu et al. single-cell dataset. (B) Trajectory analysis showing the INTS6+ ECs to occupy between PLVAP+ ECs and capillaries. (C,D) Pathways enriched in genes upregulated in INTS6+ ECs vs. other ECs in Liu et al. and Ankur sharma et al. HCC single cell dataset. (E) Pathway analysis on DEGs based on control vs INTS6 Knockdown in HUVEC cell line (F and G) Overall- and time-to-recurrence survival of INTS6+ ECs gene signature in PLANet 1.0 cohort. (H and I) Overall- and time-to-recurrence survival of INTS6+ ECs gene signature in TCGA cohort. p values were determined by kaplan-Meier survival curves and log rank test, with a significant threshold of p value <0.05. DEGs, differentially expressed genes; EC, endothelial cell; HCC, hepatocellular carcinoma; HUVECs, human umbilical vein endothelial cells; TCGA, The Cancer Genome Atlas.Fig. 4

Next, we sought to understand the differences in gene expression in INTS6+ ECs relative to other EC populations. To this end, we utilised the scRNA-seq dataset from Liu et al.29 to perform differential expression analysis. Of the 772 genes that were differentially expressed, 516 genes were upregulated in INTS6+ ECs compared to all other EC subtypes (Table S2). Importantly, we observed that several genes were strongly upregulated only in INTS6+ ECs but not in other immune and stromal cell types analysed, indicating a functional gene signature associated with this specific cell population (Fig. 4A). To determine the pathways that were over-represented among the DEGs, we performed pathway enrichment analysis. We focused on genes with a log2 fold change of at least ± 0.5 and observed that the pathways enriched in the upregulated genes included TNF-alpha signalling via NF-kB, hypoxia, complement, androgen response, and apoptosis (Fig. 4C). These findings suggest that a potential inflammatory-hypoxia process is enriched in INTS6+ ECs, which may drive recurrence. These pathways were consistently enriched in the INTS6+ ECs derived from the in-house scRNA-seq dataset from Sharma et al.22 and were also upregulated in the in-house bulk RNA-seq dataset when comparing the control vs. INTS6 knockdown condition in the HUVEC cell line (Fig. 4D,E). The consistent and coordinated activation of these molecular pathways suggests that INTS6+ ECs may influence the tumour microenvironment by remodelling the vasculature to facilitate tumour growth and dissemination.

To investigate the prognostic implications of endothelial-derived gene signatures in HCC, we identified an INTS6-centric signature characterised by the top ten upregulated genes from our prior differential expression analysis. Kaplan–Meier survival analysis was performed using the risk score calculated from Cox regression analysis in which the patients were classified into high-vs. low-risk groups using the median risk-score value for both PLANet 1.0 (n = 90) and TCGA HCC (n = 319) cohorts.4 Our results consistently indicated that the endothelial-derived INTS6 signature correlated with significantly reduced OS rates and TTR in both the PLANet 1.0 (Fig. 4F,G) and TCGA cohorts (Fig. 4H,I). We also repeated the aforementioned analysis but with a refined subset of TCGA HCC patients, including only patients with confirmed HCC, excluding all cases of mixed histology (e.g. combined HCC-cholangiocarcinoma), and removing individuals who had undergone any prior systemic or locoregional therapy. Only tumours from curative-intent surgical resections of HCC were included. This rigorous filtering process resulted in 175 samples, and the findings were consistent with the analyses conducted using the complete TCGA HCC cohort (Fig. S5A and B).

sec.title: INTS6+ ECs are enriched in areas with MVI in recurrent patients
sec.p:
MVI is a strong indicator of HCC recurrence.50 Consistently, in our PLANet 1.0 cohort, patients with MVI exhibited a shorter TTR than those without (Fig. S3). To test whether INTS6+ ECs were associated with MVI in HCC, we overlaid pathologist-annotated MVI regions on H&E images onto the CellTrek spatial co-localisation results, in which tumour cells are shown in grey and INTS6+ ECs in orange. Interestingly, these MVI regions were characterised by the pronounced presence of INTS6+ ECs (Fig. 5A). Furthermore, the primary tumours of patients with recurrence (C008T2 and C004P) consistently showed the presence of INTS6+ ECs in pathologist-annotated MVI areas (Fig. 5A). To validate this finding, we performed IF analysis on FFPE primary tumour samples from 53 patients in our PLANet 1.0 cohort with (n = 27) and without (n = 26) recurrence. We selected Stathmin 1 (STMN1) as a marker of MVI, given its well-established association with MVI.51 Our analysis revealed that the proportion of INTS6+CD31+STMN1+ ECs was higher in recurrent patients than non-recurrent patients (p = 0.036), indicating a pronounced co-localisation of INTS6+ ECs in the MVI region in the majority of patients with disease recurrence (Fig. 5B, C). Together, these findings suggest a potential role for INTS6+ ECs in promoting MVI formation and recurrence in HCC.Fig. 5
INTS6+ ECs are positively correlated with MVI in HCC.
(A) Overlaid celltrek results showing INTS6+ ECs (orange circle) and tumour cells (gray circle) on the H&E image of representative tumour sectors. Pathologist annotation for MVI on H&E images are superimposed and representative images are shown. (B) Multiplex immunofluorescence imaging of patient-derived FFPE blocks from patients with recurrent vs. non-recurrent HCC. Representative ROIs from a recurrent (HEP0853) and non-recurrent (HEP0321) patient are shown. (C) Statistical quantification of the percentage of INTS6+ ECs (CD31+INTS6+) in the MVI region (STMN1+) across 53 patients with HCC (recurrent: n = 27; non-recurrent: n = 26). EC, endothelial cell; FFPE, formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded; HCC, hepatocellular carcinoma; MVI, microvascular invasion; ROI, region of interest. Statistical comparisons between the recurrent and non-recurrent patients were conducted with the two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum test, with a significance threshold of p value <0.05.Fig. 5

sec.title: Predicted ligand-receptor interactions enriched between INTS6+ ECs and tumour cells
sec.p:
Given the close proximity of INTS6+ ECs to tumour cells, we hypothesised that INTS6+ ECs may functionally promote aggressive tumour cell behaviour. As the analysis of aggressive sectors in recurrent HCC in Fig. 3G highlighted multiple pathways essential for motility, including the RHO GTPase cycle, FAK signalling, RAF/MAP kinase cascade, growth factor-mediated EMT regulation, and VEGF signalling,[52], [53], [54], [55], [56], [57], [58], [59] we further posited that INTS6+ ECs play a pivotal role in controlling cell migration ability. To test this, we performed a migration assay using HUVECs with INTS6 knockdown, together with a Boyden chamber assay using HCC cells cultured in a transwell (Fig. 6A-G). Three different siRNA duplexes targeting INTS6 were used (Fig. 6A,B), and the siRNA that exhibited the most effective knockdown (siINTS6-1) was chosen for the transwell migration assay. Compared to siCtrl, knockdown of INTS6 in HUVECs resulted in reduced migration of HCC cells through the transwell, supporting a pro-tumourigenic role of INTS6 expressed in endothelial cells, thereby influencing tumour cell biology (Fig. 6D-G). Notably, INTS6 knockdown produced a less pronounced reduction in the migration of the moderately metastatic HCC cell line, HUH7 (Fig. 6G), compared to the other three more invasive HCC cell lines, SNU387, SNU449, and HLF. This result suggests that INTS6 dependency may be stronger in the more aggressive cell lines.Fig. 6
Functional validation and ligand-receptor interaction.
(A, B) Knockdown efficiency of siINTS6 in HUVECs was evaluated by (A) qRT-PCR and (B) western blot. (C) Migration assay in HCC cell lines cultured in transwells with HUVECs seeded in bottom wells with or without INTS6 knockdown. Statistical comparisons between the control and shINTS6s were conducted with the student t-test from 3 independent experiments. ∗ p value <0.05, ∗∗ p value <0.01, ∗∗∗ p value <0.001. (D-G) Representative images of migration assays with SNU387, SNU449, HLF, and HUH7 cells co-cultured with Control or INTS6-siRNA HUVECs. (H) Chord diagram illustrating the ligand-receptor interactions between INTS6+ ECs and tumour cells, with the thickness of the chords representing the strength of interaction. (I) Graph showing the normalized expression of ANGPTL4 and SDC1 across five different cell lines (HUH7, PLC-PRF5, SNU387, SNU449, SNU475) with Pearson’s correlation: 0.87 with p-value = 0.002. (J, K) ANGPTL4 mRNA and protein level in 293T cells measured by (J) qRT-PCR and (K) western blot after the lentiviral infection before the conditioned media was used to treat the cells in L-O. (L) Schematic of the migration assay in the presence of control media and ANGPTL4 OE-enriched media. (M-P) Migration assay results for SNU387, SNU449, HLF, and SNU475 cells treated with control media or ANGPTL4-enriched media, showing the effects on cell migration. (Q,R) Box-plot showing INTS6 and ANGPTL4 expression in INTS6 control vs. knockdown. ECs, endothelial cells; HCC, hepatocellular carcinoma; HUVECs, human umbilical vein endothelial cells; OE, overexpression; qRT-PCR, quantitative reverse-transcription PCR.Fig. 6

To ascertain the potential cell-cell interaction axes between INTS6+ ECs and tumour cells, we conducted a ligand-receptor interaction analysis on the single-cell dataset from Liu et al.. This analysis revealed several significant ligand-receptor interactions between INTS6+ ECs and tumour cells through ANGPTL4 and SDC1, COL4A1/2–SDC1, and SPP1–ITGA5/ITGB1 (Fig. 6H). Given the high statistical significance of the ANGPTL4–SDC1 interaction (Fig. 6H) and the known association of ANGPTL4 with cell motility, invasion, and SDC1 in oncogenic processes, we prioritised this interaction for further study. We overexpressed ANGPTL4 in 293T cells (Fig. 6J,K) and performed a transwell migration assay to assess HCC cell migration in response to ANGPTL4-enriched media (Fig. 6L-P). Our analysis of various HCC lines (SNU387, SNU449, and SNU475) indicated increased migration towards ANGPTL4-conditioned media compared to the control. These results highlight a novel intercellular interaction between INTS6+ ECs and tumour cells, corroborated by the enhanced invasion of HCC cells. Next, we sought to confirm the control of ANGPTL4 by INTS6 in ECs by performing bulk mRNA sequencing on HUVECs treated with either control or INTS6-targeting siRNA. As predicted, ANGPTL4 expression was significantly reduced following INTS6 knockdown, suggesting that INTS6 positively regulates ANGPTL4 expression (Fig. 6Q,R).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: In this study, we aimed to construct a spatial cellular atlas of HCC in patients with and without disease recurrence after surgery. Given the bimodal distribution of recurrence over time,9 we focused on patients who developed intrahepatic recurrence in less than 2 years, which is associated with primary tumour micrometastasis, and compared these with data from a patient who did not have recurrence 5 years after surgical resection. In the cell type distribution analysis, we observed variability in most of the annotated cell types. In particular, myeloid, fibroblast, and EC populations varied across intratumoural sectors. These observations underscore the importance of employing multi-region sampling in clinical studies that require biopsy samples for patient selection to consider profiling multiple regions of the tumour, as single-site sampling may not fully capture the cellular complexity and, thus, the biology of the tumour.60,61

Our analysis revealed a novel association between INTS6+ ECs and poor HCC prognosis following resection. INTS6+ ECs were consistently positioned in close proximity to tumour hepatocytes in the primary tumours of patients who later developed recurrence. We also identified PLVAP+ ECs in close proximity to tumour cells. This EC subtype has previously been proposed as a therapeutic target and was recently described as part of an oncofetal niche that establishes an immunosuppressive microenvironment in HCC.22,48 The INTS6 gene encodes a putative RNA helicase, and its role in EC function is poorly understood. Follow-up mechanistic studies are required to elucidate the functional properties of this endothelial subpopulation in HCC. We also identified MVI as an indicator of tumour recurrence and OS after surgical resection in patients with HCC beyond tumour burden alone.50 In our spatial transcriptomics data, the INTS6+ EC subpopulation was consistently detected within the pathologist-annotated MVI regions. Moreover, these cells were specifically enriched in the MVI-designated (STMN1+) regions of patients who later recurred, linking the presence of INTS6+ ECs to recurrence risk. The significance of these observations were further corroborated by bulk RNA-seq analysis from the PLANet and TCGA cohorts, underscoring the clinical relevance of INTS6+ ECs for predicting HCC recurrence after resection. Therefore, it is critical to dissect the underlying mechanisms by which INTS6+ ECs contribute to MVI. Are these cells merely passive markers of invasion, or do they actively participate in remodelling of the tumour microenvironment to facilitate vascular dissemination? Answering this question could open new therapeutic windows that target the vascular component of tumour progression, potentially curbing metastatic recurrence at an early stage. In addition, our ligand-receptor analysis identified a robust ANGPTL4-SDC1 interaction between INTS6+ ECs and tumour cells (Fig. 6H). A GalNAc-conjugated siRNA targeting ANGPTL3 has been developed and effectively delivered to the liver, significantly inhibiting ANGPTL3 expression and markedly reducing triglyceride and total cholesterol levels in both mouse and monkey models of dyslipidemia.62 Our in vitro results of siINTS6 and ANGPTL4 overexpression highlight the potential for developing siINTS6 or siANGPTL4 therapies for HCC.

In conclusion, our study defines the multi-region spatial transcriptomic landscape of HCC tumours with and without recurrence post-surgery. enabling neighbourhood-analyses which revealed a strong association between the co-localisation of INTS6+ ECs with tumour cells and HCC recurrence. Moreover, the spatial enrichment of INTS6+ ECs within areas of MVI in patients who subsequently recur suggests that these cells may participate in biological processes that facilitate HCC recurrence post-resection. Further experiments are warranted to validate these findings and explore the therapeutic application of targeting the INTS6 axis in the context of MVI in HCC. Beyond these specific findings, our dataset provides a valuable resource for the community to further explore pathways of interest and the associated cellular neighbourhoods that shape HCC biology. Future functional studies, using genome-wide screens and in vivo models, can be conducted to further investigate cell-cell interactions that might have clinical significance.63,64
